messages.subject: Rserve questions and "Using Rserve to get a plot()"
messages.subject_clean: Rserve questions and "Using Rserve to get a plot()"
messages.body_plain:
R appears to insist on directing plot output to a file. How do I get the results directly without having to read a file?

Is their a graphics device that keeps the output in memory that I can access using Rserve? (JavaGD?)

If I can't do this doesn't this make R and Rserve more or less useless?

I'm developing a web app for exploratory data analysis for clients using a browser. No R on their system.

To work with Rserve I have REngine.jar and RserveEngine.jar.  Is this all I need?

There's another way to use R from Java without using a server. But according to the docs I read only one instance of R per Java VM is allowed. So I can't pool it. Isn't this useless also? (Maybe I can use rmi and make a zillion independent java processes available to my web app)

Good grief.

messages.body_plain:
(I hope you did have a look at the PlotDemo example that does precisely that  ...)

On Aug 20, 2010, at 11:15 AM, Donald Winston wrote:

> R appears to insist on directing plot output to a file. How do I get the results directly without having to read a file?
> 

AFAIK all graphics devices operate either on files or on screen. So the only way to go is to have a specialized device (like xGD or JavaGD) that can map the commands to something else (if it really is soo important to you to make that sacrifice).


> Is their a graphics device that keeps the output in memory that I can access using Rserve? (JavaGD?)
> 

Not directly - note hat the big question is *what* you want in the memory. JavaGD allows you to map into Java calls so it's up to you what you do with it.


> If I can't do this doesn't this make R and Rserve more or less useless?
> 

Not really since Rserve gives you a separate working directory so there is nothing wrong with generating a file - especially since in practice the content will stay in memory anyway so speed wise the disk is not involved (and you could use ram disk if you were really concerned).


> I'm developing a web app for exploratory data analysis for clients using a browser. No R on their system.
> 

As most of us do for years ;).


> To work with Rserve I have REngine.jar and RserveEngine.jar.  Is this all I need?
> 

For the Java client, yes.


> There's another way to use R from Java without using a server. But according to the docs I read only one instance of R per Java VM is allowed.

Yes - a limitation of R.


> So I can't pool it. Isn't this useless also? (Maybe I can use rmi and make a zillion independent java processes available to my web app)
> 

You can do that (there are projects using that approach) - it's not something I'd suggest, though.

Cheers,
Simon

messages.subject: Re: RConnection close() and shutdown()
messages.body_plain:
Donald,

On Aug 29, 2010, at 11:26 AM, Donald Winston wrote:

> I'm pooling Rserve connections. 
> 

Why on Earth would you do that?


> First is is it right to assume this is desirable or necessary?
> 

I'm not sure what you mean exactly by pooling - but if you mean opening connections pre-emptively or re-using connections then, this is in general not desirable at all since most clients assume they have a new, clean connection with unpolluted workspace etc. Re-using connections is as dangerous as re-using needles - you never know what you get ;).


> There's no open() so I assume that new RConnection() "opens" a connection. Is this true?
> 

You are again very vague - so I'm assuming you are talking about the REngine-based Java client and in that case, the constructor creates a socket, connects to the server and performs the initial handshake. If you call that "open" then I suppose the answer is yes.


> Is it ok to call shutdown() without closing all the connections? (I need at least one to call shutdown()).
> 

Shutdown signals the server to tear down its listening queue and terminate gracefully. It has no effect on any open client instances - I suppose you could call that ok. (Modulo control commands - the server will tear down its end of the control pipes so clients can no longer issue control commands, but that is quite logical as there is no server process anymore).


> What would I use close() for?
> 

To close the connection and thus allow the associated child process to exit, remove temporary working directory etc.


> Kind of confusing because jdbc sql connections don't appear to work this way. (db pooling class I use handles all this stuff for me)

Rserve has pretty much nothing to do with JDBC so I fail to see any connection here...

Cheers,
Simon
